content_summary.citation: Brayden D. Bulloch (Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison), Fabio B. Gaertner (Univ. of Wisconsin-Madison), Jeffrey L. Hoopes (Univ. of North Carolina at Chapel Hill), 'Do Commercial Property Taxes Affect Business Microlocation Decisions?', The Accounting Review, published online 6 October 2026 (print date 1 Oct 2026), pp. 1-31, DOI 10.2308/TAR-2025-0248. JEL H25, H71, H73, R32.
published_abstract_findings (Crossref ab: Data: 'precise geolocations for 2.8 million U.S. establishments'.
Design: 'a spatial discontinuity density design, comparing for-profit establishments to nonprofits, which are generally exempt from property taxes'. County borders are the discontinuity.
Main result: for-profit establishments, relative to nonprofits, 'disproportionately locate on the low-tax side of county borders'; the effect strengthens with the size of the tax differential.
Effect sizes: at borders with differentials in the top decile (top quartile), 'a 6-7 (5-6) percent shift in establishment location toward the low-tax side over a 10-km band'.
Spatial pattern: businesses 'move from as far as 10 km away on the high-tax side but concentrate within 1 km on the low-tax side'.
Heterogeneity: low-foot-traffic establishments respond more to tax differentials than high-foot-traffic ones (authors: firms 'trade off tax savings with customer access').
Survey: a survey of U.S. mayors finds perceptions of property taxes' importance for business location rise with cross-border tax differentials.
working_paper_detail_Feb2024 (earlier dr: Data (WP pp. 9-11): SafeGraph Places (Dec 2022) establishment geolocations; CoreLogic Historical Property 2015-2021 (31,452,373 commercial observations) to compute county effective commercial property-tax rates as taxes paid divided by MARKET value (WP p. 10: 'dividing property taxes paid by market value for the commercial properties in the dataset'; assessed value deliberately not used); Compustat for public-firm tests. 2,609 of 3,243 counties usable (CA, CT, DE, DC, HI, MA, ME, NH, RI, VT lost to data gaps). Only within-state county borders; establishments within 10 km of a border; 2,805,455 establishments; manufacturing and medical establishments removed (abatements, non-tax siting factors). Mean county effective rate 2.1% of market value; mean border differential 0.5 percentage points (WP p. 11).

Identification (WP pp. 14-16): 303,265 nonprofit establishments (churches, schools, public buildings) as the untreated counterfactual density; 'excess' for-profit mass in a 1-km window either side of the border; net bunching = low-side excess minus high-side excess; 200 bootstrap draws; regressions with county fixed effects, SEs clustered at border level (WP pp. 20-22).

WP headline numbers (differ from the published abstract): establishments within 1 km of a border are 11 percent more likely to be on the low-tax side (WP abstract); for-profits 11.7 percent more likely than nonprofits (WP p. 3); net bunching 11.71% at the highest-differential borders and 2.67% across all borders (WP p. 18); share on the low-tax side rises from 49% to 54.7% from the lowest to highest differential groups (WP p. 14).

Heterogeneity (WP pp. 18-20): rural net bunching 7.04% vs urban 5.77%; low-foot-traffic net 7.00%, 'more than twice' the high-foot-traffic estimate. Firms with higher federal cash ETR (less income-tax planning) are more likely to sit on the low-tax side -- the authors read property-tax and income-tax planning as substitutes. Firm size, profitability and number of stores were not significant (WP pp. 24-26).

Owner-occupied vs leased premises: not examined in the WP; its literature review (WP p. 8) only notes disagreement on commercial property-tax incidence (Mieszkowski & Zodrow 1989: consumers; Man 1995 and Wheaton 1984: property owners). Industry: results pooled, mostly retail-type establishments (WP pp. 9-10); no industry split reported.
content_summary.land_vs_building: The authors' tax measure is the effective rate on the whole commercial property (land plus improvements) -- taxes paid over market value -- so the study cannot separate a land component from a building component. In the WP, searches for 'land value', 'site value', 'land tax' and 'Georg' return nothing; the framing is corporate tax planning and local-government tax competition ('local governments can weigh that importance into their considerations for how to best attract business to their counties', WP p. 27). Whether the published version says anything about site-value taxation could not be checked; the abstract does not.

implication_for_land_only_base (analysis: What it supports: jurisdiction-level differences in the effective rate on commercial property (land + buildings) shift where establishments sit at the margin, so a recurrent tax on improved commercial value is not locationally neutral. That is modern peer-reviewed evidence for the premise that taxing improved property distorts real decisions.

What it does NOT show: that a land-only base would avoid this. The response measured is to a rate DIFFERENCE between adjacent counties (tax competition / Tiebout sorting). A land tax levied at different rates by adjacent jurisdictions would create the same border incentive unless the differential is capitalised into land prices. The abstract reports establishment counts, not land prices or rents, so capitalisation is not tested; a persistent location response is, if anything, a sign that the differential is not fully capitalised within the 1-10 km band. The Georgist neutrality claim is about intensity of use within a jurisdiction (the capital-land ratio), which this design does not test.

Safe wording for the page: 'peer-reviewed evidence that commercial property-tax differentials between neighbouring counties pull establishments toward the lower-taxed side'; relevant to the business-rates-to-commercial-LVT proposal only in that a uniform national land base would remove cross-border rate differentials -- a policy inference, to be labelled as the wiki's analysis or dropped.

uncertainties: Published full text not read. Every number other than the abstract's comes from the Feb 2024 working paper, whose headline figures (11 percent, 11.7 percent, 11.71 percent net) differ from the abstract (6-7 and 5-6 percent) and whose design wording differs ('bunching' vs 'spatial discontinuity density'). The final data window, county coverage, treatment of manufacturing and medical establishments, and any new heterogeneity (owner vs lessee, industry, firm size) are unknown.
'Microlocation' here means which side of a county line, within 10 km; it is not a within-city or parcel-level siting result.

Identification relies on nonprofits as a counterfactual for where establishments would sit absent tax; the authors concede the counterfactual is imperfect (school/church siting logic). 'Percent shift' is a change in the density of establishments, not a count of firms that moved: the abstract says businesses 'move from as far as 10 km away' but the design is cross-sectional density, so relocation of existing firms is inferred, not observed (check the full text).
Effective rates are median county rates on commercial property, not parcel-specific rates; abatements and exemptions are only partly captured.
Bulloch's standing is not independently established; Tier 1 here rests on Gaertner, Hoopes and the journal.
Page numbers for quotes from the published article cannot be given; locators are to the abstract and to the WP's printed page numbers.

Scanner note framed this as 'the siting distortion a site-value tax is designed to remove'; that framing is the scanner's, not the authors', and overstates what the design shows (see land_vs_building and implication notes).

content_summary.what_it_is: A web research article by the Property Tax Lab testing Fairer Share's Proportional Property Tax (PPT) -- a flat 0.48% annual charge on current property value, paid by owners, replacing council tax and SDLT on primary residences; 0.96% on second, empty and non-resident-owned homes; transitional cap of 100 pounds a month (1,200 a year) on increases for a primary residence until sale; deferral for those unable to pay. Fairer Share's design was costed by WPI Economics (Feb 2021): PPT revenue 36.7bn = council tax 31.9bn + primary-dwelling SDLT 4.2bn + 0.6bn adjustments, 'on 2019 revenues' (Lab's phrasing; the WPI report itself, p. 3, states the 0.48% 'makes PPT revenue-neutral upon introduction' and carries a 'PRIVATE & CONFIDENTIAL' cover legend although publicly hosted).
content_summary.model_and_method: PRISM = the Lab's residential stock model. This analysis uses 'the sales sample behind PRISM': 914,742 English properties sold since 2023, each with a current-value estimate and a matched council tax band and local authority. NOTE: these are sold properties with modelled values, not 914,742 valuations of the stock. Recently sold homes are not a random sample, so winner shares and averages are computed within each council-by-band cell and weighted to the VOA's dwelling count for the cell; 301 cells with fewer than 10 sales (139,000 dwellings) borrow region-and-band results. Social homes are valued at a 26% (London) to 36% (North East) discount to private homes, calibrated to MHCLG's Market Value Survey 2024 (takes 4.4% off England's total). Each dwelling's current bill = its own council's average Band D including precepts x the statutory band ratio (A = 6/9 ... H = 18/9), compared with 0.48% of modelled value. Scope: England, bands A-H, 25.0m banded dwellings; Wales excluded.

headline_figures (all the Lab's own esti.dwellings_paying_less: 83% of dwellings (~20.7 million) pay less; average saving 784 pounds; those paying more face an average increase of 1,487 pounds (page key findings). Arithmetic checks: 20.7m / 25.0m = 82.8%.
headline_figures (all the Lab's own esti.versus_fairer_share_claim: Fairer Share claims 77% of HOUSEHOLDS (18 million) pay less, average saving 556 pounds (Fairer Share PPT page); the Lab says the measures differ (dwellings vs households, renters pay no property tax) and 'On our narrower dwelling-level test the claim holds up; if anything it is conservative.' (Fairer Share's 25 Sept 2026 release, already on the wiki's Burnham page, uses 566 pounds for the average English household -- a different release and geography, not an inconsistency in the Lab's figures.)
headline_figures (all the Lab's own esti.london_band_h: 'London Band H faces an average increase of 17,183 pounds a year; 98% of those dwellings would hit Fairer Share's 1,200-a-year transitional cap.' The table and text both give 17,183 (= 20,456 PPT less 3,273 council tax on an average 4.3m home). The scanner note's '17,173' is a transcription slip. Region-and-band table: London Band H +17,183; South West H +7,092; South East H +6,323; East of England H +6,008; Yorkshire & Humber H +5,092; North West H +4,349; West Midlands H +3,676; East Midlands H +3,313; North East Band H omitted (<30 sales). London bands C-H all net losers on average (C +58, D +486, E +932, F +1,821, G +4,300); London A -68, B -140. Outside London bands A-F mostly pay less (bar +15 on East of England F); Band G pays more everywhere except North East (-306) and East Midlands (-69).

Average change per dwelling: North East -1,078, London +962, England -391. London: 61% of dwellings pay more.
headline_figures (all the Lab's own esti.councils: Largest average savings: Hartlepool -1,353 (average value 134,255), Middlesbrough -1,332, Stockton-on-Tees -1,254. Largest increases: Kensington and Chelsea +6,128 (average value 1.74m), Westminster +5,412, Wandsworth +2,769; the ten largest increases are all London boroughs.
headline_figures (all the Lab's own esti.regressivity: Existing council tax is 1.08% of value for Band A on average versus 0.13% for Band H; the Lab says its figures show council tax 'regressive with respect to property value'.
headline_figures (all the Lab's own esti.revenue_neutral_rate: 'The 0.48% rate is stale.' On the Lab's 9.02tn valuation of England's 25.0m banded dwellings, 0.48% raises 43.3bn versus 48.3bn to replace (44.1bn council tax requirement 2025-26 + 4.2bn SDLT). Neutral rate ~0.54%; on a gross-liability (no discounts) basis gross council tax on the modelled stock is 53.1bn and the neutral rate is 0.64%. The two bounds differ because councils bill ~9bn less than full rates through the 25% single-person discount and Council Tax Support, which PPT has no equivalent of. Arithmetic checks: 9.02tn x 0.48% = 43.3bn; 48.3/9.02 = 0.535%; (53.1+4.2)/9.02 = 0.635%. Council tax requirements up ~38% since 2019 (the Lab's figure); primary-residence SDLT ~5bn in 2024-25 versus the 4.2bn WPI used.
headline_figures (all the Lab's own esti.transitional_cap: 1.3 million dwellings (5.3% of stock) exceed the cap; first-year cost ~3.5bn (~8% of gross PPT yield); 74% of relief goes to London (52% to London G and H). Design flaw per the Lab: the cap ends on sale, re-creating a moving penalty for the largest-increase households (London Band H owner pays 4,473 under the cap but the buyer faces 20,456). Lab suggests a decade-long time-based taper. The Lab notes WPI says the cost of the protection is 'already factored into' the 0.48% but publishes no figure.
headline_figures (all the Lab's own esti.stamp_duty: SDLT replacement IS included in the revenue arithmetic (4.2bn, 2019 vintage) and has a separate efficiency section: +8.8% transactions on abolition (~76,343 extra sales a year, using OBR semi-elasticities), 804m of deadweight loss removed per year, 16,032 additional long-distance movers. For an average London Band G buyer, SDLT saved 98,107 once vs ~4,299 a year more tax; exhausted after ~23 years. Details are on the Lab's separate Stamp Duty page (not read).

assumptions_and_caveats_stated_by_the_La: Gross liability basis: 'Council Tax bills are modelled at full rates. Single-person discounts (25%), Council Tax Support, exemptions and premiums are not modelled on either side', so Fairer Share's household-level winner shares are not directly comparable and single occupants' increases are understated.
SDLT is 2019-vintage (4.2bn); 'main-residence SDLT raised nearer 5bn in 2024-25', so the shortfall and neutral rates are slightly understated.
Average Band D including precepts per authority; no parish-level variation.

Social-housing valuation approximate; too many social homes placed in upper bands within a council, so band-level winner splits within a region are less certain; for social homes the PPT would fall on the landlord while the tenant pays council tax today.
Within-cell selection bias from using recently sold homes: stratification removes between-cell bias, not residual within-cell bias.
The 0.96% surcharge on second/empty/non-resident homes is not modelled and would claw back some of the shortfall; values move (a 2029 start on 2028 values would shift every figure, not the pattern).

Design reservations (Our Assessment): sale-triggered cap; renters and incidence ('moving legal liability to owners does not settle who ultimately pays'); deferral for asset-rich cash-poor owners; revenue volatility with market values; valuation 'solvable but not free'.

existing_wiki_coverage: The Lab is NOT cited on any wiki page by URL; sources/registry.csv has no row for it; it is not in people-tiers.json. Where it appears: research/muellbauer-property-tax-reform-england.md, 'Revenue and Reach': 'Using Michael Dent's Property Tax Lab estimates -- about 159,000 English homes above 2m (average value 3.61m) and 172,000 between 1.5m and 2m (average 1.71m), from 2024-25 transactions matched to stock totals and updated to mid-2026 with Nationwide indices -- and assuming 80%/20% and 90%/10% primary/second-home splits ... the paper puts revenue at 2.01bn ... 0.2bn ... 2.21bn in total', footnoted [1] to Muellbauer; and under Limits: 'its revenue figures rest on a single consultancy's stock estimates'. The Sources section lists only the Muellbauer paper. Assessment: 4c-compliant -- the Lab is a Tier 2 data input, named as the source of the stock estimates, carried through a Tier 1 paper, not used as support for anything, and flagged as single-source. Three small improvements for T1: (a) 'consultancy' is inaccurate (the Lab describes itself as independent data and policy analysis; Dent founded the property-data firm PropertyData) -- say 'a single independent modeller's stock estimates (Michael Dent's Property Tax Lab)'; (b) state Dent's status once, impersonally; (c) the current PRISM page now shows ~163,000 homes above 2m (values indexed to Q2 2026) against Muellbauer's 159,000, so the page should keep the figures attributed to Muellbauer's paper and not update them from the live model. Muellbauer's cite of the Lab's PPT page (Dent 2026b) and acknowledgement are not mentioned on the wiki page and need not be. Other coverage of the Fairer Share design: people/andy-burnham.md (para at line 29: 0.48%/0.96%, 270,000-pound home paying about 1,296, regional price effects, Telegraph via Yahoo Finance [11]; line 31: i Paper 28 July 2026 area savings, 1,200-pound cap and deferral; line 41: Fairer Share's own 25 Sept 2026 modelling -- 566 pounds average, 279 of 295 authorities, 10.1bn -- 'rest on its own 2020-based household modelling ... with no independent review' [20], c-claim); places/united-kingdom.md line 32 (0.48% replacing council tax and SDLT, 'on the order of 35 billion pounds a year' [5], Goodhart's transition warning); research/resolution-foundation-home-economics.md (RF's 0.7% occupier-paid tax; Fairer Share named as promoting the same base; RF's neutral rate 0.66%/0.7% against a 74bn 2030-31 target and 10.9tn stock -- not comparable with the Lab's 0.54-0.64% on a 9.02tn 2025 stock replacing 48.3bn). suggested_enrichment_sentences: people/andy-burnham.md (after the line-41 paragraph; attribute, no grade codes): 'The Property Tax Lab, an independent research site on English and Welsh residential property taxes founded by Michael Dent (founder of the property-data firm PropertyData), tested the 0.48% design against a reweighted sample of 914,742 recent English sales and reported, in its own modelling, that 83% of dwellings (about 20.7 million) would pay less than under council tax, against 39% in London, where the average Band H home would pay about 17,183 pounds a year more; 98% of those Band H homes would reach the 1,200-pound transitional cap.' Then: 'It also found the rate calibrated on 2019 revenues: on its valuation of England's homes 0.48% raises 43.3 billion pounds against 48.3 billion to replace (council tax requirement 44.1 billion, MHCLG, plus 4.2 billion of stamp duty), putting a revenue-neutral rate at 0.54% to 0.64% depending on whether discounts are counted; its calculations exclude the 0.96% surcharge and the 25% single-person discount.' Add a Sources entry 'used for ...' with the C-claim grade and a note that the analysis is the Lab's unreviewed modelling, publicised by the campaign.

places/united-kingdom.md (clause after the 'on the order of 35 billion pounds' figure): 'a figure calibrated on 2019 revenues; one independent modelling exercise puts the amount to be replaced at about 48 billion pounds on 2025-26 figures (council tax requirement 44.1 billion plus 4.2 billion stamp duty).' Anchor the 44.1 billion to MHCLG.
uncertainties: No publication date, byline or version history on the page; appeared by 28 Sept 2026. The page is live and can change (the PRISM model page already shows a different count of 2m+ homes from the one Muellbauer used).

The Lab's independence is self-declared; its founder is a property-data entrepreneur and the analysis was welcomed and promoted by Fairer Share (28 Sept post, which reports the 83% finding and the 'if anything conservative' line and says the neutral rate would be 'higher' but omits the 0.54-0.64% numbers and the London Band H figure). No evidence of commissioning or funding by the campaign was found; none was looked for beyond the About page.

'914,742 valuations' in the scanner note is shorthand for modelled values of 914,742 recent sales, reweighted to the VOA stock; winner shares are therefore model outputs with residual within-cell selection bias, as the Lab states.

Dwelling-level, gross-liability comparison: not comparable with Fairer Share's household-level 77% and likely understates losses for single occupiers (25% discount) and for council tax support recipients.
The scanner note's '+17,173' for London Band H is wrong; the page says 17,183 in both text and table.
The Lab's 25.0m dwelling base differs from the VOA's ~25.7m English properties (Lab excludes annexes, park homes and uncovered cells); effect on rates is small but not nil.
Charts (distribution of bill changes, share paying less by band, effective rate by band) are not machine-readable; only tables were read.
Whether the Lab or Dent is cited by any other Tier 1 body is unknown; the search found nothing, but search coverage was thin.

uncertainties: All substantive content unknown; the only reliable facts are bibliographic.

Whether the article is peer-reviewed in a conventional sense, its method (e.g. time series on turnout/seat shares vs GDP or oil rent), and whether it finds that rent distribution 'breaks' the economic vote cannot be stated.

Kuwait's elections before 1992 were restricted-franchise and often suspended (parliament suspended 1976-81 and 1986-92 per general knowledge, not checked here), which would make a 1975-2020 series methodologically delicate; this is a reason for care, not a finding about the paper.
Scanner note's framing ('reward or punish governments') may not match the paper's actual question.
